sections.description: Introduces the coolant system concept and the idea that coolant is a mixture (approximately 50% water and 50% ethylene glycol). States the ideal engine temperature around 200 F / 90 C and notes that the cooling system's purpose is to keep hot engine parts from overheating, with the radiator acting as the heat sink.
sections.title: Coolant system overview and 50/50 coolant mix

concepts: pump placement at front of engine
coolant flow: radiator bottom -> engine block -> cylinder head -> radiator
thermostat controls flow based on temperature
sections.description: Describes the pump’s location on the front of the engine, driven by a belt from the crankshaft, and outlines the coolant’s loop through the engine and back to the radiator. Explains that the thermostat regulates flow to the radiator depending on engine temperature.
sections.title: Water pump location, basic operation, and coolant flow path

sections.description: Notes that the pump typically runs at a fixed ratio to engine RPM and points out the limitation of this arrangement, setting up the discussion of electric water pumps as a more flexible alternative.
sections.title: Pump speed and fixed drive ratio; lead-in to electric pumps

concepts: electric pumps offer flexible flow control and mounting
sections.description: Explains why some manufacturers use electric water pumps for better flow control and placement, and introduces heat soak—the engine temperature can rise briefly after shutdown because cooling ceases. Mentions hybrids and stop-start systems as drivers for electric pumps.
sections.title: Electric water pumps and heat soak concept

sections.description: Shows that the pump is sealed for life and typically replaced as a whole unit (except the pulley) and reveals that the bearing is integrated into the shaft and lubricated at the factory.
sections.title: Water pump internals and why pumps are replaced as units

concepts: Weep hole as a discharge path
sections.description: Details the mechanical seal construction (two faces with a micron clearance) and the Weep hole that allows small amounts of liquid to escape, which can be a normal feature or a sign of issues if coolant leaks are excessive.
sections.title: Mechanical seal, Weep hole, and leakage diagnostics

concepts: seal leaks due to bearing failure
sections.description: Outlines three main failure modes: leaks from a worn seal (often bearing-related), bearing noise, and impeller failure or corrosion leading to reduced flow.
sections.title: Common Water-pump failure modes

summary: The video from How a Car Works explains the role of the water pump in a typical automotive cooling system, using a Mazda MX-5 Miata as the exemplar. It covers coolant composition (roughly 50/50 water and ethylene glycol), the closed cooling loop path from radiator to engine and back, and the thermostat’s role in regulating flow. The pump is shown as belt-driven and mounted at the front of the engine, driving the coolant through the engine and to the radiator. The internals are explored—an impeller inside a volute, a shaft-driven bearing, and a mechanical seal with a Weep hole—along with common failure modes. The video contrasts belt-driven pumps with electric pumps, discusses heat soak after engine shutdown, and notes maintenance practices such as replacing the pump as a unit during timing belt service. Practical diagnostic cues and model examples (BMW, Audi, Prius/Lexus hybrids) are highlighted to illustrate the varying implementations in modern cars.
title: Water Pump Anatomy and Operation in a Car Cooling System
